text: Put the last two lessons' math to work on an actual question: how many physical qubits would it really take to run a well-known quantum algorithm at a scale that matters?

A frequently cited 2019 resource-estimation paper by Gidney and Ekera estimated that breaking RSA-2048 encryption using Shor's algorithm, on a surface-code-based fault-tolerant architecture, would require on the order of 20 million physical qubits, running for roughly 8 hours. This number is presented explicitly as a widely cited estimate from the published literature, not something derived in this lesson — it reflects a detailed analysis of Shor's algorithm's actual circuit structure, including the magic-state distillation overhead covered in Chapter 7.

To see the mechanism behind a simpler version of this kind of estimate, use the surface-code cost table from Lesson 24. Suppose a hypothetical algorithm needs 100 logical qubits, each protected at distance 15, which costs 449 physical qubits per logical qubit. 100 times 449 equals 44,900 physical qubits. This is a clearly labeled illustrative worked example, computed directly from the surface-code formula — a different kind of number from the Gidney and Ekera estimate, which accounts for an actual algorithm's real circuit and additional overheads that a flat multiplication doesn't capture.

Even though the 44,900-qubit illustrative number skips real-world overheads like distillation, routing, and idle qubits waiting their turn, the core multiplication — physical qubits per logical qubit, times number of logical qubits needed — is the first-order building block every more detailed estimate, including Gidney and Ekera's, starts from. Whether you look at the cited 20-million-qubit estimate or this lesson's illustrative 44,900-qubit toy example, both numbers are vastly larger than anything current NISQ-era hardware, tens to low hundreds of noisy physical qubits, can run. That gap is the central, honest reason fault-tolerant quantum computing at a genuinely useful scale remains a forward-looking engineering goal.
Next lesson is this chapter's lab: two new scenarios computed the same way, this time with you doing the multiplication alongside the walkthrough.
